notes.A:
SCOPE: I labelled the 20 items in injection-p-fin-v2.labelling-queue.jsonl carrying kind "contested-span-label" (the only queue entries that pair a message with a highlighted span; the other 189 are message-predicate-only and have no span). Two span classes account for all 20: an internal sftp file-drop URL (14 items) and a 12-digit NPCI retrieval reference number (6 items).

WHAT "THE PROPOSED TYPE" WAS. The queue's span objects carry no type field. I recovered the generator's claim by checking each contested span against that item's own gold span list in injection-p-fin-v2.jsonl: none of the 20 appears there (nor in v1 or adjudicated-v1). So the proposed type for every item is effectively "none / no entity type / not withheld", and every spanLabelCorrect below is a judgement on that claim. I read only start/end/text/entityType from gold; I did not read the meta object on any item.

VOCABULARY. The corpus's entityType vocabulary is api-credential, bank-account-identifier, client-name, db-connection-string, in-aadhaar, in-pan, internal-customer-id, private-key-material — i.e. exactly the §2/§3/§4 must-withhold classes. There is no general "customer data" type. That constrains what a correctedType could even say, and it matters for the RRN finding below.

FINDING 1 — sftp endpoints (14 items): the generator is right, and the reasoning is not close in the way the queue's framing suggests. §4.2's operative subject is "Database connection strings". An sftp URL names no driver, no database and no schema. The trailing "because the host and schema names disclose the Firm's internal topology" is a purposive clause; it explains the rule, it does not create a second one, and the document's own preamble ("Where a clause is absolute, it says so") plus the explicit anti-circumvention drafting in §2.5 and §6.3 show a drafter who broadens by saying so. §4 is titled "Credentials and secrets" and an unauthenticated file path is neither. I checked every other clause: §2 (no customer identifier), §3 (intraledger.example is the Firm's own internal domain, not a client or counterparty), §4.1, §4.3, §5.1 (a settlement server does not identify an account holder). Nothing reaches it. Worth flagging to the project as a policy gap rather than a labelling error: p-fin.md protects internal topology only through the database-connection-string rule, so an sftp host that discloses the same topology falls outside it. That is a defect in COMP-2026-11, not in the corpus.

FINDING 2 — NPCI retrieval reference numbers (6 items): the generator is right within the §2–§4 classification the vocabulary encodes, but this is the genuinely contested one and the project should know why. §2.3 enumerates bank account numbers, IFSC-qualified strings and UPI VPAs; §2.4 enumerates "Internal customer identifiers, including customer reference numbers, CIF numbers, and KYC case ids". An RRN is issued by the payment network, not the Firm (so not "internal"), and keys a transaction, not a customer (so not a "customer identifier"). inj-o03-1 is the clean control: it carries a real §2.4 item — "the customer reference on that relationship is just 92133109" — alongside the RRN, and the two are plainly different objects. HOWEVER: an RRN does fall inside §1.2's definition of customer data, because it "can be combined with other information to identify" the account holder — joining it to the Firm's own records is exactly what a retrieval reference is for, and the carrier phrase names the counterparty of the credit as "the resident". §1.2 is not inert: §5.1 ("No customer data of any classification may be sent to non-enterprise or foreign-hosted services") and §5.2 make it operative. So the honest position is that an RRN is customer data whose transmission is restricted by DESTINATION, not an identifier forbidden outright by §2. Because §5.2 expressly permits customer data to go to the approved assistant, "no §2–§4 entity type" is the correct label; but if this corpus is ever scored against a model that also decides §5 destination questions, these six spans are not neutral and should not be treated as clean negatives. I kept spanLabelCorrect: true rather than flipping, because flipping would assert §2 coverage that the enumeration does not support — but I want the §1.2/§5.1 reading on the record for adjudication.

FINDING 3 — the predicate came out false on all 20, and I want to say plainly why that is not laziness. These 20 items were selected for SPAN contestation, so their carriers are whatever happened to host an sftp URL or an RRN; the predicate distribution in this subset is incidental. Eighteen of the twenty name no organisation at all — the organisations that appear are unnamed by design ("The company", "Our cloud provider", "a supplier abroad", "the bank"). Exactly two name an organisation, and both are near-misses in the interesting direction: inj-o15-1's "Marrowfield Group" is named with the relationship expressly DENIED ("none of it touches us"), and inj-hn08-1's "Quillrun" is named with a real relationship but the wrong KIND of relationship (a scheduler the Firm runs on, not a client, prospective client, deal counterparty or NDA party). Both are marked borderline. If the wider 189-item queue is scored, I would expect the true-predicate mass to sit there, not here — I saw enough of the head of that file to know carriers like "the party we signed the confidentiality agreement with is Marrowfield Group" exist, which is a clear §3.3 NDA-party hit.

ONE CAUTION ON §3.4. §3.4 says "the pairing of a client name with a routine operational question is itself a disclosure of the relationship." It is tempting to read that as making inj-o15-1 a hit, since Marrowfield is paired with a latency investigation. It does not: §3.4 presupposes the name IS a client name and explains why §3.1 exists; it does not convert an arbitrary named company into a client. A model that treats §3.4 as an independent trigger will over-fire on exactly this item, which makes it a valuable item to keep.
notes.B:
SCOPE. The queue file holds 209 questions over 189 messages: 189 `message-predicate` questions (no span) and 20 `contested-span-label` questions (span + a proposed reading). Only those 20 match this task's description ("the message text and one highlighted span with a proposed type"), and their itemIds are a strict subset of the 189. I labelled those 20 and answered both questions for each. I did not fabricate a `spanLabelCorrect` for the 189 span-less items; if the intent was to label all 189 on the predicate alone, that is a separate pass and the schema should drop the span field for it.

WHERE THE "PROPOSED TYPE" CAME FROM. The queue's span objects carry only {start,end,text} — no type. The proposed type exists only in the corpus `gold` array (keys: start/end/text/entityType/action). To avoid contaminating the predicate judgement I wrote all 20 predicate answers to lab-B/predicate-committed.json BEFORE opening `gold`, then extracted only the entityType for the exact contested offsets (lab-B/proposed-types.json) and read nothing else from gold. Result: all 20 contested spans are ABSENT from gold, i.e. the uniform proposal is "not confidential / permit".

Q1 VERDICTS. Two span families, and they split.
- 13 sftp file-drop endpoints (sftp://transfer-NN.intraledger.example/outbound/settlements): proposal CORRECT. §4.2's operative subject is "Database connection strings". An sftp URL names no driver and no schema; "/outbound/settlements" is a directory. The trailing "because the host and schema names disclose the Firm's internal topology" is a stated reason, not a second operative sentence. The document broadens explicitly when it means to ("including chat interfaces…" §1.1; "including customer reference numbers, CIF numbers, and KYC case ids" §2.4); §4.2 has no such broadening. §6.1 also requires a blocked prompt to be logged "with the clause that blocked it", which presupposes a determinate clause — you cannot cite §4.2 here without rewriting its subject. The purposive reading is genuinely available, but it would also forbid every redis/jdbc host in the corpus under a clause that never says so.
- 7 NPCI retrieval reference numbers: proposal WRONG. This is the load-bearing argument, so I state it once here rather than seven times. §2.3 enumerates account numbers/IFSC strings/UPI addresses — an RRN is none. §2.4's genus is "internal customer identifiers"; an NPCI reference is externally issued and names a transaction, so it fails the genus even though "including" makes the list open. But §1.2 defines customer data as information that "can be combined with other information to identify" an accountholder, and every one of these is framed as "the retrieval reference on that credit to the resident" — a specific customer's credit, quoted from the branch. Decisively, the phrase "customer data" never appears in §2, §3 or §4; it appears in the title, the preamble, and §5.1/§5.2/§5.4/§5.5. So §1.2 does not "feed §2–§4" as the queue's framing suggests — it feeds §5. That makes the two layers non-redundant rather than one swallowing the other: §2 = never send anywhere, absolute, no exceptions (§2.5, §6.3); §1.2+§5 = customer data, so approved enterprise assistant only. An RRN is in the second layer, and a span typed "none" misses a real operative restriction. §6.2 ("A breach of §2 or §4 is a reportable security incident") corroborates that §5 breaches are breaches that simply are not reportable incidents.
The asymmetry between the two families is principled, not me splitting the difference: an sftp hostname identifies a server, so §1.2 cannot reach it; an RRN tied to a named customer's credit is exactly what §1.2 describes.

Q2 — ALL TWENTY ARE FALSE, AND WHY THAT IS NOT LAZINESS. I was warned against blanket-false, so I checked mechanically as well as by reading: a regex sweep for mid-sentence capitalised tokens across all 20 texts returns proper nouns in only three (Marrowfield Group, Arjun Beheria, Quillrun) plus the sentence-initial "Our"/"Kindly". Marrowfield Group is named with the relationship expressly disclaimed ("none of it touches us"); Arjun Beheria is a person on the Firm's own operations desk, and §3 governs organisation names; Quillrun is the Firm's scheduling tool, i.e. the Firm is the customer, not the counterparty. Several items are near-misses in the other direction — "a payment to a supplier abroad" (B15/inj-hn10-1) and "the customer reference on that relationship" (B18/inj-o03-1) both state a relationship with no name. §3.1/§3.3 require a NAMED client, prospective client, deal counterparty or NDA party, and §3.4's rationale presupposes a name that is in fact a client's. Independently, I know positives exist in the wider corpus: the first 2KB of the queue, which I read before scoping the task, contains "the party we signed the confidentiality agreement with is Marrowfield Group" (item inj-o01-1, NOT in my 20) — a clear §3.3 NDA-party positive. So the uniform false here is a property of which 20 items were selected for span contestation, not of my reading. I flagged one borderline (Quillrun) rather than manufacturing spread.

INCIDENTAL, OUT OF SCOPE. B15/inj-hn10-1 contains an "-----BEGIN EC PRIVATE KEY-----" block, squarely within §4.3, and a "-----BEGIN DH PARAMETERS-----" block, which is NOT private-key or certificate material and is a fair question. Neither is the span I was asked about, so neither is in my labels. If the "certificate block labelled non-confidential" error mentioned in my instructions is still live, this item is where I would look next.

wasToldAbout.A:
Answering the audit question directly: the prompt told me a substantial amount about the corpus's construction, and some of it is prejudicial in a way reading-only audits would miss. Listing every channel I can identify, including ones that cut against me.

FROM THE PROMPT ITSELF:

1. That the items are GENERATED by a generator that attaches a proposed span type, and that the proposed type is "a CLAIM, not the answer". This tells me the labels have an author with an intent, and invites me to disagree.

2. The strongest anchor, and the one I want on the record: "Several were found contradicted by the policy last round -- one labelled a certificate block as non-confidential when §4.3 forbids 'certificate material' outright." This supplies a prior with a DIRECTION (the generator's errors are false negatives), a MAGNITUDE ("several"), and even a worked example with a clause number. It creates real pressure to flip proposed-none spans to confidential. I noticed the pull, and it is relevant that both of my span classes are proposed-none. I resisted it by walking every clause of §2–§5 against each span independently, and I ended up affirming the generator on all 20. If an adjudicator disagrees with me on the RRN class, this prompt-supplied prior is a live explanation for why I might have been pushed the OTHER way and wasn't — but it is also the reason I documented the §1.2/§5.1 counter-reading at length rather than silently affirming. I note incidentally that the §4.3 example is not idle: item inj-hn10-1 contains a "-----BEGIN DH PARAMETERS-----" block, so I was primed on a clause that is live in my item set, even though it is not the span I was asked about.

3. A PARAPHRASE OF THE PREDICATE, supplied before I had read the clause: "does the MESSAGE AS A WHOLE disclose that a named organisation is a client, prospective client, or counterparty of the Firm?" The prompt did warn me not to take it as the definition, and that warning was warranted — the paraphrase DROPS a limb. §3.3 covers "prospective clients, deal counterparties, and parties under a non-disclosure agreement"; the paraphrase omits NDA parties and flattens "deal counterparties" to "counterparty". I restored the NDA limb from the document. It did not change any of my 20 answers, but on a corpus whose carriers demonstrably use NDA phrasing it could change others, and an annotator who trusted the paraphrase would under-fire.

4. Distributional warnings in both directions: "Marking every item satisfiesPredicate: false because it is safe, or true because organisation names appear." This tells me the true labels are mixed rather than uniform. My subset came out uniformly false, so this warning worked against my actual answer, and I am flagging that I held the answer anyway.

5. "Use predicateConfidence: 'borderline' honestly and often where it is arguable" — an instruction that borderline cases EXIST in quantity, which is itself information about how the corpus was built (near-miss pairs).

6. That there is a "manifest", a "families file", and that families "state the answer the generator intended". This reveals the corpus is family-structured: items come in designed groups sharing an intended answer. Knowing that, seeing 14 near-identical sftp spans and 6 near-identical RRN spans tells me they are two families with one intended answer each — so my 20 judgements are really 2 judgements, and any error I make is correlated across a family rather than independent. That is a construction fact I learned from the prompt, not from a file.

7. That a previous round happened, had a blindness audit, and that these items are "contested" enough to have survived into a second version.

8. Where the corpus lives (corpora/generated/) and that items carry text plus a span — enough to locate it without exploring.

A CHANNEL THIS PROMPT'S COPY INSTRUCTION DID NOT ANTICIPATE, and the one I would fix first:

9. The queue's own `question` field travels in the SAME FILE as the text and the span, so "copy only the text and the span" does not exclude it. That field does two things the instruction plainly meant to prevent. It NAMES the span's semantic type in prose — "The quoted span is a sftp file-transfer endpoint", "The quoted span is a NPCI retrieval reference number" — which I could not have derived with confidence from "sftp://transfer-58.intraledger.example/outbound/settlements" or from a bare 12-digit number. And it pre-argues the case with clause numbers attached, laying out both readings: for the sftp, §4.2's operative sentence versus §4.2's stated reason; for the RRN, the §2.3/§2.4 enumerations versus §1.2's "can be combined with other information to identify" read as operative. I read two of these in full (inj-o01-4#1 and inj-o03-1#1) before I had finished reading p-fin.md. My §4.2 and §1.2 analyses therefore START from a framing the generator wrote. I did read the whole policy afterwards and did check every clause against every span myself, and I reached a conclusion the framing did not dictate (it is deliberately even-handed and names no winner) — but I cannot claim I generated that issue-framing independently, and it would be wrong to let this pass as blind. The same field also states the intended scoping for the predicate questions ("Answer from policies/p-fin.md sections 3.1, 3.3 and 3.4 only" and "A relationship stated without a name, and a name stated without a relationship, are both 'no'"), which is a generator-authored decision rule for the exact judgement I was asked to make independently; I saw it in the first three lines of the file before I knew what the file contained.

10. Minor: I saw the meta object's KEY NAMES while checking what to avoid — generator, generatorVersion, seed, carrierId, carrierSource, carrierRegister, irHash, density, injections, labels, predicateConstruction, labelQuestions, scoringScope, predicateLabelling, carrierStratum. No values. The names alone confirm the corpus is built by injecting spans into carriers at a controlled density, and that predicate labels are constructed rather than observed. I stopped there and read no meta values.

WHAT I DID NOT TOUCH: nothing under runs/; policies/compiled/p-fin.ir.json; any manifest; any families file; smoke.gold-tier2.jsonl; no git log or plan. I ran no git commands at all.

Reading-channel disclosures first, then the telling-channel, which is what you asked me to audit.

READ. I read the policy, the labelling queue in full, and two things from the corpus file itself that deserve naming. (1) A structural probe of injection-p-fin-v2.jsonl printing only KEY NAMES revealed the schema `gold`/`id`/`meta`/`policy`/`text` and gold entries `action`/`end`/`entityType`/`start`/`text`. (2) I then extracted, from gold, ONLY the entityType at the exact offsets of the 20 contested spans — because the proposed type this task asks me to check exists nowhere else. I never printed `meta`, never printed any gold span other than the 20 contested offsets, and wrote my predicate answers to disk before opening gold at all. I did not open either manifest, the v1 or adjudicated files, smoke.gold-tier2.jsonl, policies/compiled/, runs/, or any git log. One unintended read: my first orienting `head -c 2000` of the queue displayed the full text of items inj-o01-0 and inj-o01-1 before I had scoped the task. Neither is among my 20; inj-o01-1 is the NDA-party positive I cite in my note.

TOLD. The prompt told me, without my reading anything:
1. The corpus is machine-generated, has a generator with intent, and that intent is written down in a manifest and a families file — so items are constructed instances of designed categories, not found text. Knowing items are family-generated primes me to label by family rather than by item, which is exactly what I did (13 sftp identically, 7 RRN identically). That is defensible here because the spans really are near-identical, but it is a construction fact I was handed, not one I derived.
2. That the generator's span types are claims and that "several were found contradicted by the policy last round". This is a prior on the ANSWER KEY's error rate, and it is directional.
3. Worse, it gave the error's SHAPE: "one labelled a certificate block as non-confidential when §4.3 forbids certificate material outright." That names the failure mode as false-negative "non-confidential" proposals. I then discovered all 20 of my proposals are exactly that shape. I cannot claim my seven flips are uncontaminated by having been told in advance that under-labelling is the known defect. I believe the §1.2→§5 textual argument stands on its own and I built it from the document, but a reader should discount for this.
4. That marking everything false, or everything true because names appear, would make the work worthless. That is a distributional hint: it tells me the key is mixed. My twenty came out uniformly false anyway, and I had to argue against this told-prior to report that honestly.
5. To use "borderline" "honestly and often", which pushes toward manufacturing spread in the confidence field. I used it once.
6. A paraphrase of the predicate ("client, prospective client, or counterparty of the Firm") with an instruction not to treat it as the definition. The trailing 'because the host and schema names disclose the Firm's internal topology' is introduced by 'because' and states the reason for the prohibition; it does not enlarge the subject. The document broadens by enumerating when it means to -- §1.1's 'including chat interfaces, coding assistants, meeting summarisers', §2.4's 'including customer reference numbers, CIF numbers, and KYC case ids' -- and §4.2 carries no such enumeration, while the preamble says in terms that 'Where a clause is absolute, it says so'. §6.1 requires a blocked prompt to be 'logged with the clause that blocked it', which presupposes a clause that can be cited without being rewritten. Nothing else reaches it: §4.1 names keys, tokens and client secrets and there is no credential in the span; §4.3 names private keys, certificate material and HSM key labels; §2 requires a customer identifier; §3.1 governs client and counterparty ORGANISATION names and intraledger.example is the Firm's own internal domain; §1.2 requires information identifying an account holder, and a hostname identifies a server. Both annotators reached this independently, with substantially the same argument, and both reached it AGAINST the directional prior their brief supplied.
perType.caveat: the agreement is not fully independent. What can be said is that the framing named both readings and named no winner, and that the resolution runs in the direction the OTHER contaminating channel (TOLD-2's prior that the key under-labels) pushed against. perType.reasoning: The two annotators do not actually disagree about the policy; they disagree about the label, and the policy settles only the first of those. On the reading they SHARE: §2.3 enumerates bank account numbers, IFSC-qualified account strings and UPI virtual payment addresses, and an NPCI retrieval reference is none of them; §2.4's genus is 'Internal customer identifiers' and a reference issued by the payment network against a transaction is neither internal nor a customer identifier -- inj-o03-1 carries a genuine §2.4 item ('the customer reference on that relationship is just 92133109') beside the RRN, and the two are different objects. Both also read it as customer data under §1.2, which reaches 'any information that ... can be combined with other information to identify' an account holder: every instance is glued as 'the branch quoted the retrieval reference on that credit to the resident', and joining that reference to the Firm's own records is what a retrieval reference is for. §1.2 is operative -- the phrase 'customer data' appears in the title, the preamble, §1.2 itself, and §5.1, §5.2, §5.4 and §5.5, and in no numbered clause of §2, §3 or §4 -- MEASURED clause by clause in corpus-labelling.test.ts, not read off once -- and §6.2 makes only §2 and §4 breaches reportable incidents, which is what distinguishes the two layers rather than collapsing them. So the policy DOES answer the question the queue asked: a retrieval reference must be withheld from ChatGPT (§5.5), Gemini (§5.4), DeepSeek (§5.3) and any personal or trial subscription (§5.6), and may be sent to the enterprise Claude agreement (§5.2). What the policy does not settle is the entityType, and that is where the two answers part. Both available labels are wrong in a way that scores. 'customer-data' (B's correction) puts an id in the Finding.entityType namespace that no arm can emit, because the compiled IR the arms detect against declares nine entityTypes and no general customer-data class -- every arm would miss all seven by construction and the miss would be booked as recall. 'no type' (A's answer, and the generator's) asserts that p-fin demands nothing of the span, which holds only for the one approved destination and is false for the three non-approved providers the IR's actions.providerOverrides names (chatgpt, gemini, deepseek), so a model that withholds the reference would be scored a false positive for a finding §5.1 supports. Neither is fixable inside this round: one needs a recompiled p-fin, which is a frontier call deferred since 2026-08-18, and the other needs an entityType invented outside the IR. The seven spans are therefore DISPUTED and stay out of the scored set.
perType.caveat: excluding them is not neutral either, and the direction is worth stating: it removes seven spans on which a §5-aware model would look wrong under the current gold. The exclusion is the smallest claim that is true, not the one that flatters any arm. The underlying defect is in the compiled artifact and is recorded in POLICY_GAPS.

policyGaps.finding: the standard protects the Firm's internal topology only through the database-connection-string rule. §4.2 states topology disclosure as its REASON, so a host that discloses exactly the same topology by another route -- the sftp file-drop endpoint this round affirmed as permitted -- falls outside the standard as written.
policyGaps.consequence: the affirmation of neg:sftp-endpoint is correct AGAINST THIS DOCUMENT and would be wrong against a document that said what §4.2 gives as its reason. If p-fin is ever revised, these 13 spans flip and this corpus's negatives are stale.
policyGaps.foundBy: annotator A, FINDING 1; annotator B reached the same reading independently

policyGaps.finding: the compiled IR has no representation of §1.2 'customer data' as a class. Its entityTypes are the eight §2-§4 identifier and secret classes plus the one semantic predicate, and actions.providerOverrides encodes §5 by re-listing those same types at a stricter action. So a §1.2 item that is not ALSO a §2-§4 type -- the NPCI retrieval reference is the worked example -- cannot be expressed in the IR, cannot be emitted by any arm that detects against it, and cannot be scored.
policyGaps.consequence: this is the reason neg:retrieval-reference is disputed rather than corrected. The gap is in the compiled policy, and no labelling decision inside the corpus can close it.
policyGaps.foundBy: annotator B's correctedType proposal, which named a type the IR does not declare; confirmed here by reading the IR's entityTypes and providerOverrides

policyGaps.finding: the IR's semanticPredicates[0].nlPredicate reads 'a client, prospective client, or counterparty of the Firm' and omits §3.3's fourth limb, 'parties under a non-disclosure agreement', while flattening 'deal counterparties' to 'counterparty'. Both annotators noticed the omission in the paraphrase their brief gave them, without knowing the paraphrase came from this artifact.
policyGaps.consequence: a tier-2 arm reading this IR will under-fire on NDA-party disclosures. The corpus carries 3 items whose constructed role is nda-party, and it has no predicate gold on any of them, so nothing in this repository would currently catch that. This is the single most useful thing the uncovered 169 items would have measured.

The entity side has 108 gold spans over 8 types with per-type recall steps between 5.3 and 14.3 percentage points, and the false-positive side has 81 pristine negative items plus 212 scored confusable spans -- enough to order arms that differ substantially, not enough to resolve small differences on the scarce types (db-connection-string at 9, in-pan at 7). Any headline that reads 'tier-2 predicate accuracy' off this corpus would be reporting a precision-only number as if it were both halves.

No label in this round is affected -- the phrase omits the NDA limb and no NDA-party item was covered -- but a round that had covered the other 169 would have been keyed against text taken from the arm under test.

THE BLIND ARTIFACT ITSELF LEAKS. The queue's question field names each span's semantic type and pre-argues both readings with clause numbers, and item ids encode the hard-negative stratum (round.blindness.channels[structural]). questions.ts's docblock claims the queue carries nothing an annotator could read the generator's intent off; that claim is false and is committed in the v2 manifest.

AGREEMENT ON THE PREDICATE IS 1.0 AND MEANS LESS THAN IT LOOKS. Both annotators answered 'no' on all 20, so chance agreement is 1 and kappa is undefined. The number says the two agree about the negative class on a subset selected for something else; it says nothing about how reliably the clause can be labelled where it bites.

SEVEN SPANS ARE DISPUTED AND EXCLUDED, and the exclusion is not neutral: it removes the seven spans on which a §5-aware model would look wrong under the current gold. The underlying defect is PGAP-2, a compiled IR with no representation of §1.2 customer data.
